readings.challenge: Listen to the Fox’s reasons, and then to the one reason the old fox gives for doubting them.
readings.focus: The Fox tries to make everyone share his loss so that he will not feel ashamed.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. The trap is a hunter’s trap that snaps shut. A stump is the short piece left. Inconvenient means awkward or in the way. An encumbrance is something heavy and useless to carry; to dispense with something is to do without it; an ornament is a decoration. Interested advice is advice that helps the one who gives it.
readings.contentNote: The Fox loses most of his tail in a trap.

excerpt.locator: “The Fox Without a Tail,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “It happened that a Fox caught its tail in a trap, and in struggling to release himself…”; closes “Distrust interested advice.”.

questions.prompt: How does the Fox lose his tail, and how does he feel at first?
facilitatorNotes: In a trap; he is ashamed to be seen.
evidence: At first he was ashamed to show himself among his fellow foxes.

questions.prompt: What reasons does he give for all foxes doing away with their tails?
facilitatorNotes: Tails are in the way when dogs chase them and when foxes sit down to talk, and a tail is useless to carry.
evidence: how inconvenient a tail was when they were pursued by their enemies, the dogs

questions.prompt: What does the older fox notice?
facilitatorNotes: That the Fox thinks tails useless only because he has lost his own. The advice is for the giver’s sake.
evidence: if you had not happened to lose it yourself

questions.prompt: Why might the Fox want every fox to lose its tail? What would have been a better way to face his trouble?
facilitatorNotes: So no one would look different from him or laugh at him. He might have told the truth and carried on; some children will feel sorry for him. Ask whether his “bolder face” was brave or sly.
evidence: he determined to put a bolder face upon his misfortune

readings.title: The Hare and the Tortoise
readings.challenge: Notice how the Hare and the Tortoise each talk before the race.
readings.focus: Steady work beats a speed that stops to show off.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A tortoise is a slow animal with a shell that lives on land. To boast is to brag. A challenge is a dare to a contest. Contempt is looking down on someone. To plod is to walk slowly and steadily. The winning-post marks the end of the race.

excerpt.locator: “The Hare and the Tortoise,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “The Hare was once boasting of his speed before the other animals. “I have never yet been…”; closes ““Plodding wins the race.””.

questions.prompt: What does the Hare boast about, and how does the Tortoise answer?
facilitatorNotes: That he has never been beaten. The Tortoise answers quietly that it accepts. Ask how the two voices should sound.
evidence: I have never yet been beaten
The Tortoise said quietly

questions.prompt: Why does the Hare lie down for a nap?
facilitatorNotes: To show how little he thinks of the Tortoise; he is sure he will win anyway.
evidence: to show his contempt for the Tortoise, lay down to have a nap

questions.prompt: The fable says the Tortoise “plodded on and plodded on.” What does that tell you about how it won?
facilitatorNotes: It never stopped. Saying the words twice makes the slow steps feel long and steady; read them slowly.
evidence: The Tortoise plodded on and plodded on

questions.prompt: Was the Tortoise faster, or did the Hare lose the race by himself?
facilitatorNotes: The Hare was much faster and lost by stopping. Some children will say the Tortoise won by never giving up, others that the Hare beat himself; both fit “Plodding wins the race.”
evidence: Plodding wins the race.

readings.title: The Hare With Many Friends
readings.challenge: Count the friends the Hare asks, and listen to each one’s excuse.
readings.focus: Friends who each pass her on to the next leave the Hare to save herself.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Hounds are hunting dogs. To decline is to say no politely. An appointment is a meeting fixed for a certain time. A ram is a male sheep, and a calf a young cow or bull. To repel is to drive back. To take to your heels is to run away.
readings.contentNote: Hunting dogs chase the Hare; she escapes.

excerpt.locator: “The Hare With Many Friends,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Hare was very popular with the other beasts who all claimed to be her friends. But one…”; closes “He that has many friends, has no friends.”.

questions.prompt: How many friends does the Hare ask for help? Name them in order.
facilitatorNotes: Five: the horse, the bull, the goat, the ram and the calf.
evidence: she went to the horse
applied, as a last hope, to the calf

questions.prompt: Each friend says no and names someone else who will surely help. Why do they all do that?
facilitatorNotes: It lets each one say no without feeling bad. Every excuse sounds polite, and none of them helps.
evidence: that all her other friends would come to her assistance

questions.prompt: Which excuse is the silliest? Which is the most honest?
facilitatorNotes: Children may choose the bull’s appointment, or the calf, who will not help because older animals would not. The ram is the most honest: he is afraid of the hounds himself. Accept reasons tied to the words.
evidence: I have an appointment with a lady
hounds have been known to eat sheep as well as hares

questions.prompt: The moral says, “He that has many friends, has no friends.” Is that true for the Hare? Is it always true?
facilitatorNotes: For the Hare, yes: all of them together helped less than one true friend would. Many children will say it is not always true; ask what makes a real friend.
evidence: He that has many friends, has no friends.

readings.title: The Bundle of Sticks
readings.challenge: Watch what changes between the father’s two orders, “Break it” and “Now, break.”
readings.focus: A father shows his sons, without a speech, why they should stay together.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A faggot is a bundle of sticks tied together. On the point of death means about to die, and parting advice is what someone tells you as they leave you. Union means being joined together.

excerpt.locator: “The Bundle of Sticks,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “An old man on the point of death summoned his sons around him to give them some parting…”; closes “Union gives strength.”.

questions.prompt: What happens when the sons try to break the whole bundle?
facilitatorNotes: None of them can, though the eldest strains and strains.
evidence: with all his efforts was unable to break the Bundle

questions.prompt: What is different the second time?
facilitatorNotes: The bundle is untied, each son has one stick, and each stick breaks easily.
evidence: each stick was easily broken

questions.prompt: The father says, “You see my meaning.” What is his meaning, and why does he show it instead of just saying it?
facilitatorNotes: Together the brothers are strong; apart, each is easy to break. Showing lets them feel it in their own hands, so they will remember. Some children will add that he wants them not to quarrel after he is gone.
evidence: You see my meaning
Union gives strength.

readings.title: The Lion, the Fox, and the Beasts
readings.challenge: Look at the ground with the Fox and work out what happened inside the cave.
readings.focus: The Fox reads the footprints and stays outside.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Sick unto death means so ill he is about to die. A will, or last Will and Testament, says who gets your things when you die. To pay your respects is to make a polite visit. Toils are nets or traps.
readings.contentNote: The Lion pretends to be dying so that animals will come into his cave, and they never come out. The fable only hints that he eats them.

excerpt.locator: “The Lion, the Fox, and the Beasts,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “The Lion once gave out that he was sick unto death and summoned the animals to come and…”; closes “It is easier to get into the enemy’s toils than out again.”.

questions.prompt: Which animals go into the Lion’s cave, and what does he say he wants them for?
facilitatorNotes: A Goat, a Sheep and a Calf, to hear his last wishes.
evidence: summoned the animals to come and hear his last Will and Testament

questions.prompt: What clue does the Fox see on the ground?
facilitatorNotes: Many hoof-marks going in and none coming out.
evidence: while I see many hoof-marks going in, I see none coming out

questions.prompt: What does the clue tell you about the Goat, the Sheep and the Calf, and about the Lion’s sickness?
facilitatorNotes: They never came out: the Lion caught them, and he only “seemed” to be sick. The fable lets the listener work it out.
evidence: But soon the Lion seemed to recover

questions.prompt: The Fox answers the Lion very politely. Why doesn’t he just call him a liar?
facilitatorNotes: The Lion is dangerous and close by; polite words keep the Fox safe while he still says no. Some children will think him cheeky. His words are polite and his meaning is not.
evidence: I beg your Majesty’s pardon

readings.title: The Cat-Maiden
readings.challenge: Listen for the test each god uses to prove a point.
readings.focus: A cat may look like a bride, but she still chases mice.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. In old Greek and Roman stories Jupiter is the king of the gods and Venus the goddess of love. Disputing means arguing. A maiden is a young woman. Becomingly means nicely and properly. “Nature will out” means that what you really are shows in the end.

excerpt.locator: “The Cat-Maiden,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “The gods were once disputing whether it was possible for a living being to change its…”; closes ““Nature will out.””.

questions.prompt: What question are Jupiter and Venus arguing about?
facilitatorNotes: Whether a living thing can change its nature, what it really is inside. Jupiter says yes; Venus says no.
evidence: whether it was possible for a living being to change its nature

questions.prompt: How does Jupiter try to prove he is right?
facilitatorNotes: He turns a Cat into a Maiden, gives her to a young man for a wife, and points out how nicely she behaves at the feast.
evidence: Who could tell that yesterday she was but a Cat?

questions.prompt: What does Venus do, and what happens?
facilitatorNotes: She lets a mouse loose, and the bride jumps up to pounce on it. Venus needs only a minute.
evidence: Wait a minute
tried to pounce upon the mouse

questions.prompt: Do you agree that “Nature will out”? Can people change what they are like?
facilitatorNotes: The fable says no. Many children will say people can change habits, such as learning to share, even if some things stay. Accept either, tied to the cat’s pounce.
evidence: Nature will out.

readings.title: The Buffoon and the Countryman
readings.challenge: Notice what the crowd thinks it hears, and what it really hears.
readings.focus: The crowd cheers the copy and hisses at the real thing.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A country fair is a market with shows and games. A buffoon is a clown. To imitate is to copy. A porker is a pig, and concealed means hidden. A countryman lives and works on the land. The spectators or audience are the people watching. To hiss is to make an angry “sss” at a performer.
readings.contentNote: The Countryman pinches a little pig’s ear to make it squeal, and the crowd throws stones at him.

excerpt.locator: “The Buffoon and the Countryman,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “At a country fair there was a Buffoon who made all the people laugh by imitating the…”; closes “Men often applaud an imitation and hiss the real thing.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the crowd laugh and cheer the Buffoon?
facilitatorNotes: He copies animal cries, and his pig’s squeak is so good they think he has a pig hidden on him.
evidence: the spectators thought that he had a porker concealed about him

questions.prompt: What does the Countryman promise to do?
facilitatorNotes: Come back the next day and show them what a pig’s squeak is really like.
evidence: You give me till tomorrow and I will show you what it’s like.

questions.prompt: Why does the crowd hiss and throw stones at the Countryman?
facilitatorNotes: They think his squeal is a hideous copy, though it is a real pig. They expected the clown to be the good one.
evidence: squealed so hideously that the spectators hissed

questions.prompt: Why is the crowd foolish? And was it fair to the little pig?
facilitatorNotes: They praise the copy and hate the real sound, so they were not really listening. Some children will be upset that the pig’s ear was pinched; that is fair to say, and the fable does not stop to care.
evidence: Men often applaud an imitation and hiss the real thing.

readings.title: The Fox and the Goat
readings.challenge: Listen to the Fox’s story, and ask why he tells it.
readings.focus: A Fox in trouble gives advice that helps only himself; then the book ends with a cheer.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A well is a deep hole dug down to water. A drought is a long time without rain, when water runs short. The very last line is not part of the fable: it is Jacobs saying goodbye at the end of his book.
readings.contentNote: The Fox leaves the Goat stuck in the well.

excerpt.locator: “The Fox and the Goat,” the whole fable with its moral, and the book’s closing line; opens “By an unlucky chance a Fox fell into a deep well from which he could not get out. A Goat…”; closes “And this is the end of Æsop’s Fables. HURRAH!”.

questions.prompt: How did the Fox really get into the well, and what does he tell the Goat?
facilitatorNotes: He fell in by accident, but tells the Goat he jumped in on purpose to have water during a drought.
evidence: By an unlucky chance a Fox fell into a deep well
so I jumped down here in order to be sure to have water by me

questions.prompt: How does the Fox use the Goat to get out?
facilitatorNotes: He jumps on her back and steps on her long horns to reach the edge.
evidence: by putting his foot on her long horns

questions.prompt: Why should the Goat have doubted the Fox’s advice?
facilitatorNotes: He was stuck and needed help, so anything he said might be meant to get himself out. Some children will say she should have asked why he was really down there.
evidence: Never trust the advice of a man in difficulties.

questions.prompt: The book ends “HURRAH!” Who is speaking now, and why might he cheer?
facilitatorNotes: Not the Fox: it is Jacobs, who retold the fables, cheering at the end of the whole book, and perhaps the listener too. Ask the child which fable was a favourite.
evidence: And this is the end of Æsop’s Fables. HURRAH!
